Agents & Agentic LLMs

A research-level guide to decision processes, tool learning, search, memory, interfaces, agent training, orchestration, and reliable evaluation.

1. The core problem: act correctly when the state is only partly known

An agentic LLM is a policy embedded in a feedback system. It chooses an action, receives an observation, updates its representation of the task, and decides whether to continue. The action may retrieve information, run code, edit a repository, manipulate a browser, ask another model, or change external state. The research problem is reliable task completion under partial observability and a finite resource budget. Producing a plausible transcript is not the objective; the desired state of the world must actually be reached.

This distinction changes the failure model. A wrong answer in a single completion is one failure. A wrong action can alter the environment, consume a budget, destroy evidence, or make later observations misleading. A timeout may mean an operation failed, or that it succeeded but its response was lost. A retrieved page may contain useful facts and adversarial instructions together. A model may reason coherently from an obsolete screenshot. Long-horizon performance depends on how the entire loop handles these cases.

The field developed through several overlapping research lines: grounding language in tools; searching over alternatives; storing experience and skills; designing environments and interfaces; optimizing prompts, programs, and policy weights; coordinating specialized resources; and evaluating reliability. This guide follows landmark contributions and their variants within those lines. Original paper figures are used to explain mechanisms, not as decoration. Historical benchmark scores are labeled by setting because current models and harnesses change quickly.

TransitionLandscape contributionsNew capabilityCore unresolved issue

2. Foundations: state, policy, action, observation, and termination

The environment state is not the transcript

Let s be the real environment state, o an observation, a an action, and h the interaction history. A policy conditions on h or a compressed representation of it. In a partially observed problem, two histories can look similar while hiding different states: an item may already have been purchased, a file may have changed in another process, or an API may have returned stale data. The agent's internal task state is therefore an estimate, not the world itself.

at∼πθ(⋅∣goal,ht,memory),st+1∼P(⋅∣st,at),ot+1∼O(⋅∣st+1,at),ht+1=update⁡(ht,at,ot+1),J(π)=E ⁣[Uterminal−λ∑tcost⁡(at)−μTelapsed−failure penalties].\begin{aligned}a_t&\sim\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid\mathrm{goal},h_t,\mathrm{memory}),\\s_{t+1}&\sim P(\cdot\mid s_t,a_t),\\o_{t+1}&\sim O(\cdot\mid s_{t+1},a_t),\\h_{t+1}&=\operatorname{update}(h_t,a_t,o_{t+1}),\\J(\pi)&=\mathbb E\!\left[U_{\mathrm{terminal}}-\lambda\sum_t\operatorname{cost}(a_t)\right.\\&\qquad\left.-\mu T_{\mathrm{elapsed}}-\mathrm{failure\ penalties}\right].\end{aligned}at​st+1​ot+1​ht+1​J(π)​∼πθ​(⋅∣goal,ht​,memory),∼P(⋅∣st​,at​),∼O(⋅∣st+1​,at​),=update(ht​,at​,ot+1​),=E[Uterminal​−λt∑​cost(at​)−μTelapsed​−failure penalties].​

A formal belief state b(s) is a probability distribution over possible environment states. A Bayesian update combines the transition model and observation likelihood. Most LLM systems do not maintain this distribution explicitly; they use summaries, structured records, tool results, and heuristics. The belief-state view remains valuable because it reveals when a missing observation matters. If the agent cannot distinguish “action failed” from “action succeeded,” repeating the action is a decision under uncertainty rather than a harmless retry.

A useful task state records goals, constraints, established facts with provenance, completed artifacts, pending operations, dependencies, tool identifiers, and unresolved uncertainty. The full transcript is an audit trail; a compact state representation supports decisions. Summarization can reduce context cost but may remove a constraint needed many steps later. State maintenance should preserve invariants and references to evidence, not merely produce a fluent narrative.

Four types of correctness

Syntactic correctness means the call matches a schema. Semantic correctness means its arguments identify the intended objects. Procedural correctness means the action is valid in the current workflow and policy. Outcome correctness means the final environment satisfies the user's objective. Function calling mainly helps the first layer. A perfectly valid JSON request can still refund the wrong order, edit the wrong file, or stop after completing only half the task.

Termination is an action too. The policy should distinguish “the tool returned success” from “the requested outcome has been verified.” A compiler exit code does not prove a software issue is fixed. A browser button click does not prove the server committed the change. Verification often requires a fresh read of state or a domain-specific test. The stopping rule should depend on observed completion criteria and remaining uncertainty, not on how complete the answer sounds.

Workflow, reactive controller, planner, and search

Control structureWho chooses the next operation?Best suited toTypical failure
Fixed workflowProgrammed dependency graphKnown task families with stable interfacesCannot adapt when an unexpected observation changes the route
Reactive loopModel after every observationExploration and tasks with unknown intermediate stateRepeated calls, drift, unnecessary serial reasoning
Planner–executorModel proposes subgoals; executor follows and revisesMulti-stage tasks with explicit dependenciesStale plans and misunderstood subtask contracts
Search controllerAlgorithm explores candidate partial solutionsReversible or simulated environments with useful evaluationBranch explosion or evaluator exploitation
Multi-agent controllerSeveral policies coordinate through messages/artifactsDecomposable work requiring distinct evidence or toolsCorrelated mistakes, communication overhead, merge conflicts

These structures are composable. A fixed outer workflow can contain a reactive research step; a search procedure can call tools; a planner can delegate independent subtasks. The appropriate baseline is the simplest structure that captures the task's actual dependencies. Adding another agent creates another communication and state-management problem, so the improvement must be measured against a matched resource budget.

Value of information: when should the agent make another call?

A tool call has value when its observation can change a consequential decision. Suppose an agent can finish now with expected utility U, or obtain observation o and then choose an action. The expected value of information is the improvement from conditioning that choice on o, minus the cost and latency of obtaining it. This frames retrieval, verification, and escalation as decision problems rather than habits.

VOI⁡(tool)=Eo ⁣[max⁡aE[U(a,s)∣h,o]]−max⁡aE[U(a,s)∣h]−cost⁡(tool).Execute when benefit exceeds resource and risk costs.\begin{aligned}\operatorname{VOI}(\mathrm{tool})&=\mathbb E_o\!\left[\max_a\mathbb E[U(a,s)\mid h,o]\right]\\&\quad-\max_a\mathbb E[U(a,s)\mid h]-\operatorname{cost}(\mathrm{tool}).\\&\text{Execute when benefit exceeds resource and risk costs.}\end{aligned}VOI(tool)​=Eo​[amax​E[U(a,s)∣h,o]]−amax​E[U(a,s)∣h]−cost(tool).Execute when benefit exceeds resource and risk costs.​

For example, a repository agent has two plausible locations for a bug. Reading a small relevant function may resolve the ambiguity at low cost; asking three large models to speculate from the same issue description may add little information. Conversely, once a deterministic test proves a patch fails, more verbal debate about its plausibility has low value compared with inspecting the failing trace. The equation explains why better observation selection can outperform simply increasing reasoning length.

The quantities are rarely known exactly, so a practical controller uses approximations: uncertainty, expected information gain, tool reliability, and task stakes. These approximations must be calibrated. Entropy in the model's next-token distribution is not automatically uncertainty about the environment; a model can confidently describe the wrong state. A useful evaluation logs which calls changed the eventual decision and which merely repeated evidence already present.

Stopping follows the same logic. If completion is established by a strong check and remaining calls are unlikely to uncover a meaningful defect, the expected value of further work can be negative. If an essential constraint is still unverified, a fluent final answer should not terminate the process. This is a principled reason to make completion tests explicit before execution, so the controller can distinguish productive investigation from open-ended continuation.

Derivation: information is valuable when it changes a decision

State and assumptions. Let s be the environment state, h the observed history, and b(s)=P(s|h) the agent's belief. A tool action a can change state through T(s′|s,a) and return o through likelihood O(o|s′,a). When these distributions are known, Bayes filtering is:

b′(s′)=O(o∣s′,a)∑sT(s′∣s,a)b(s)∑uO(o∣u,a)∑sT(u∣s,a)b(s),V0(b)=Ustop(b),VH(b)=max⁡ ⁣{Ustop(b),max⁡a[−c(a)+EoVH−1(update⁡(b,a,o))]},H≥1tool steps remaining.\begin{aligned}b'(s')&=\frac{O(o\mid s',a)\sum_sT(s'\mid s,a)b(s)}{\sum_uO(o\mid u,a)\sum_sT(u\mid s,a)b(s)},\\V_0(b)&=U_{\mathrm{stop}}(b),\\V_H(b)&=\max\!\left\{U_{\mathrm{stop}}(b),\max_a\left[-c(a)+\mathbb E_oV_{H-1}(\operatorname{update}(b,a,o))\right]\right\},\\&\hspace{1em}H\ge1\quad\text{tool steps remaining}.\end{aligned}b′(s′)V0​(b)VH​(b)​=∑u​O(o∣u,a)∑s​T(u∣s,a)b(s)O(o∣s′,a)∑s​T(s′∣s,a)b(s)​,=Ustop​(b),=max{Ustop​(b),amax​[−c(a)+Eo​VH−1​(update(b,a,o))]},H≥1tool steps remaining.​

The first expression predicts the state after the action, then conditions on the returned observation. A database mutation is therefore different from a read-only diagnostic. The Bellman expression compares stopping with paying for another action and continuing; a terminal utility can incorporate whether the desired environment change actually occurred. This is an ideal decision-theoretic model, not a claim that an LLM explicitly represents calibrated state probabilities.

For a read-only tool followed by one final decision d, define utility u(d,s). Without the tool, the best expected value is max_d E_bu(d,s). With the tool, the decision may depend on o. Its gross value of information is:

VOIgross=Eo ⁣[max⁡dE[u(d,s)∣h,o]]−max⁡dE[u(d,s)∣h],VOInet=VOIgross−cost⁡(tool).\begin{aligned}\mathrm{VOI}_{\mathrm{gross}}&=\mathbb E_o\!\left[\max_d\mathbb E[u(d,s)\mid h,o]\right]-\max_d\mathbb E[u(d,s)\mid h],\\\mathrm{VOI}_{\mathrm{net}}&=\mathrm{VOI}_{\mathrm{gross}}-\operatorname{cost}(\mathrm{tool}).\end{aligned}VOIgross​VOInet​​=Eo​[dmax​E[u(d,s)∣h,o]]−dmax​E[u(d,s)∣h],=VOIgross​−cost(tool).​

Gross value is nonnegative under the model because the informed decision maker can ignore o and use the original best decision. Formally, E[max_d Z_d]≥max_d E[Z_d], and the law of total expectation recovers the original utility. Net value can be negative after cost, latency, or risk. If the tool changes the state, the pure-information formula no longer isolates its effect; use the transition-aware value equation.

Entropy reduction is not the same objective. A tool can reveal many irrelevant bits without changing any useful action. Conversely, a single bit about whether an operation already committed can prevent an expensive duplicate action. An inaccurate observation model can also make apparent information harmful in practice, despite the theorem for a correctly specified Bayesian decision maker.

Exercise — Should the agent run another diagnostic?

A failure is server-side with probability 0.6 and client-side with probability 0.4. Choosing the correct repair gives utility 1; the wrong repair gives 0. A read-only test is positive with probability 0.9 for a server fault and 0.2 for a client fault. The test costs 0.05 utility. Calculate the best expected utility before and after the test.

Show worked solution

Without the test, choose server repair for expected utility 0.6. Positive-test joint masses are 0.54 server and 0.08 client, so P(positive)=0.62 and P(server|positive)=0.54/0.62≈0.871. Negative-test masses are 0.06 server and 0.32 client; choose client repair after a negative result.

Utility with information=0.54+0.32=0.86,VOIgross=0.86−0.60=0.26,VOInet=0.26−0.05=0.21,Utility after test cost=0.81.\begin{aligned}\text{Utility with information}&=0.54+0.32=0.86,\\\mathrm{VOI}_{\mathrm{gross}}&=0.86-0.60=0.26,\\\mathrm{VOI}_{\mathrm{net}}&=0.26-0.05=0.21,\\\text{Utility after test cost}&=0.81.\end{aligned}Utility with informationVOIgross​VOInet​Utility after test cost​=0.54+0.32=0.86,=0.86−0.60=0.26,=0.26−0.05=0.21,=0.81.​

The optimal decision switches with the test outcome, which creates the gain. If both outcomes still favored the same repair, the diagnostic could reduce uncertainty without improving this immediate decision.

3. 2020–2022: from knowledge augmentation to ReAct

RAG and MRKL establish external computation as part of the system

RAG conditions generation on retrieved passages. The retriever decides what evidence is visible, and the generator decides how to use it. The retrieval distribution therefore acts as an information bottleneck: a generator cannot reliably cite a document never retrieved, and a strong retriever does not ensure faithful synthesis. Retrieval evaluation should separate finding a relevant passage, finding sufficient evidence, and producing an answer supported by that evidence. [1]

MRKL proposes modular routing between a language model and specialized components such as calculators or information sources. The conceptual change is that the model need not approximate every operation internally. It can choose a component with a more appropriate computational contract. A calculator gives exact arithmetic for its input; it does not decide whether that input represents the user's real problem. The interface between language and specialized computation becomes a central learning problem. [4]

CoT prompting supplies examples of intermediate reasoning, while self-consistency samples several reasoning paths and aggregates their answers. These techniques add inference-time computation but do not necessarily acquire new external evidence. Majority agreement is useful only when correct answers are more likely and errors are sufficiently diverse. Ten copies of the same misconception are not ten independent confirmations. [2] [3]

ReAct: interleave reasoning and actions so evidence can change the trajectory

ReAct alternates language reasoning, environment actions, and observations. A reasoning step can identify missing information or interpret a tool result; an action can retrieve evidence that revises the next reasoning step. This reduces the tendency of an uninterrupted language-only chain to elaborate an unsupported premise. The key contribution is the coupling between inference and observation, not a particular label such as “Thought:” in a prompt. [5]

The original figure compares standard answering, reasoning-only, action-only, and combined ReAct trajectories. In the question-answering example, external search resolves a factual dependency that a language-only chain can get wrong. In the interactive environment example, reasoning interprets what an observation implies for the next action. Read the highlighted errors as examples of failure mechanisms, not a statistical proof from two anecdotes; the paper's task-level experiments provide the aggregate evidence.

A minimal ReAct controller contains an action parser, a tool executor, an observation formatter, a context update, and a stopping condition. Every one can change performance. Truncated search output may hide the answer; an ambiguous tool description may cause repeated misuse; a parser may silently convert an invalid call into a different valid one. The model and harness form a joint policy, so swapping the harness while naming only the model is not a complete experimental description.

ReAct also exposes a latency tradeoff. If every small action requires a full model round trip over a growing history, serial overhead and repeated input tokens can dominate. Some observations are genuinely necessary before planning the next step; others are independent lookups that could be scheduled together. Later planning and compiler methods target this unnecessary serial dependence while retaining feedback where it is needed.

ReWOO and LLMCompiler: make dependencies explicit

ReWOO separates a planner that produces tool-use steps with symbolic references, workers that execute those steps, and a solver that composes the results. The planner can describe later operations using variables for earlier outputs before seeing those outputs. This avoids repeatedly sending the entire reasoning history to a large model. It works best when the dependency structure is predictable; unexpected evidence can require replanning. [34]

LLMCompiler converts function calls into a dependency graph, dispatches operations when inputs become available, and executes independent calls concurrently. The critical path, rather than the sum of all call latencies, becomes the ideal latency bound. The paper reports up to 3.7× latency improvement and 6.7× cost savings in its evaluated tasks, which depend on the amount of exploitable parallelism and the baseline's repeated reasoning overhead. [35]

Tserial≈∑iTi+Torchestration,TDAG≥max⁡p∈dependency paths∑i∈pTi.Speedup is limited by dependencies, rate limits, contention,and the cost of discovering or correcting the plan.\begin{aligned}T_{\mathrm{serial}}&\approx\sum_iT_i+T_{\mathrm{orchestration}},\\T_{\mathrm{DAG}}&\ge\max_{p\in\text{dependency paths}}\sum_{i\in p}T_i.\\&\text{Speedup is limited by dependencies, rate limits, contention,}\\&\text{and the cost of discovering or correcting the plan.}\end{aligned}Tserial​TDAG​​≈i∑​Ti​+Torchestration​,≥p∈dependency pathsmax​i∈p∑​Ti​.Speedup is limited by dependencies, rate limits, contention,and the cost of discovering or correcting the plan.​

A plan is not a guarantee that calls are independent. Two writes to the same object can conflict even if their arguments do not syntactically depend on one another. A search followed by a mutation may need a freshness check. A professional scheduler distinguishes read-only information gathering, isolated computation, and state-changing operations, using explicit dependency and consistency rules rather than assuming every available tool can run in parallel.

Derivation: the dependency graph gives two distinct parallelism lower bounds

Represent tool calls as a directed acyclic graph. Node i takes time tᵢ, edges encode required input or state-order dependencies, and P identical workers can run at most P calls at once. Assume durations are known, calls are nonpreemptive, and there is no resource contention beyond worker count. Define total work W=Σᵢtᵢ and critical-path length L=max_pathΣᵢ∈pathtᵢ.

  1. Work bound. In time T, P workers can execute at most PT units of work, so T≥W/P.
  2. Dependency bound. Calls on one path cannot overlap, so T≥L regardless of worker count.
  3. Combined limit. Every valid schedule therefore satisfies T≥max(W/P,L). Relative to ideal serial work W, speedup is at most min(P,W/L).
Tparallel≥max⁡ ⁣(WP,L),Speedup=WTparallel≤min⁡ ⁣(P,WL),Tend to end=Tplanning+Tscheduling/execution+Tintegration.Represent any overlap explicitly in the graph.\begin{aligned}T_{\mathrm{parallel}}&\ge\max\!\left(\frac WP,L\right),\\\mathrm{Speedup}&=\frac W{T_{\mathrm{parallel}}}\le\min\!\left(P,\frac WL\right),\\T_{\mathrm{end\ to\ end}}&=T_{\mathrm{planning}}+T_{\mathrm{scheduling/execution}}+T_{\mathrm{integration}}.\\&\text{Represent any overlap explicitly in the graph.}\end{aligned}Tparallel​SpeedupTend to end​​≥max(PW​,L),=Tparallel​W​≤min(P,LW​),=Tplanning​+Tscheduling/execution​+Tintegration​.Represent any overlap explicitly in the graph.​

The bound is not always attainable: precedence constraints can leave workers idle even when remaining work exists. Under the simplified assumptions, standard greedy list scheduling has a useful upper bound W/P+(1−1/P)L, obtained by charging fully busy intervals to work and underfilled intervals to a dependency chain. Real services add rate limits, heterogeneous runtimes, failures, and queueing; those invalidate an unqualified equality with the lower bound.

LLMCompiler exploits a graph that exposes independent calls. Its benefit depends on whether the graph is known before observations arrive. If a diagnostic changes which calls are needed, static parallelization can execute unnecessary work. Also, two writes can have a semantic conflict even when neither consumes the other's textual output. A dependency graph must include those state constraints to preserve behavior.

Exercise — Find a schedule and its speedup ceiling

Calls A and B take 2 and 3 seconds and are initially ready. C takes 4 seconds after A. D takes 1 second after both B and C. With two workers, compute W, L, a valid optimal schedule, and the benefit of adding a third worker.

Show worked solution
W=2+3+4+1=10 s,L=max⁡(A→C→D,B→D)=max⁡(2+4+1,3+1)=7 s,Tparallel≥max⁡(10/2,7)=7 s.\begin{aligned}W&=2+3+4+1=10\,\mathrm s,\\L&=\max(A\to C\to D,B\to D)\\&=\max(2+4+1,3+1)=7\,\mathrm s,\\T_{\mathrm{parallel}}&\ge\max(10/2,7)=7\,\mathrm s.\end{aligned}WLTparallel​​=2+3+4+1=10s,=max(A→C→D,B→D)=max(2+4+1,3+1)=7s,≥max(10/2,7)=7s.​

Run A and B at time 0. A finishes at 2 and C runs from 2 to 6. B finishes at 3. D runs from 6 to 7. This meets the bound, so it is optimal under the assumptions. A third worker cannot shorten the 7-second chain. Ideal speedup over serial is 10/7≈1.43×, before graph construction and answer-integration overhead.

4. 2023: Toolformer learns when a tool is useful

Self-supervision from reduction in future-token loss

Toolformer generates candidate API calls at possible insertion points in text, executes them, and retains calls whose results improve prediction of subsequent text. The model is then finetuned on the augmented corpus. This turns a small set of tool demonstrations into a larger training signal without requiring a human to label every call. It learns trigger timing, API choice, arguments, and how to incorporate a returned result. [6]

Li(z)=−∑j≥iwj−ilog⁡pM(xj∣z,x<j),Li+=Li(encoded call + result),Li−=min⁡[Li(no call),Li(call without result)],Keep ifLi−−Li+≥τfilter.\begin{aligned}\mathcal L_i(z)&=-\sum_{j\ge i}w_{j-i}\log p_M(x_j\mid z,x_{<j}),\\\mathcal L_i^+&=\mathcal L_i(\text{encoded call + result}),\\\mathcal L_i^-&=\min[\mathcal L_i(\text{no call}),\mathcal L_i(\text{call without result})],\\\text{Keep if}\quad\mathcal L_i^--\mathcal L_i^+&\ge\tau_{\mathrm{filter}}.\end{aligned}Li​(z)Li+​Li−​Keep ifLi−​−Li+​​=−j≥i∑​wj−i​logpM​(xj​∣z,x<j​),=Li​(encoded call + result),=min[Li​(no call),Li​(call without result)],≥τfilter​.​

The second baseline matters. If the call text itself reveals the upcoming answer, a filter comparing only against no call could reward a useless API invocation. Comparing with the call without its result asks whether the external result contributes additional information. The weighted future-token loss emphasizes nearby consequences. This is a clever automatically measurable proxy, but it values tools that improve text prediction, which need not match the utility of a real task.

Read the original pipeline as candidate generation → execution → filtering → augmented training data. In the example, two candidate questions produce different API results, and the loss test decides which result helps the continuation. The green/red filtering terms expose the causal comparison. The process does not learn by updating a policy after each real user task; it constructs a supervised dataset from tool-enriched text and then trains on that dataset.

Derivation: Toolformer’s filter is a weighted likelihood-ratio test

Fix the future tokens that the filter attempts to predict. Let p₊,ⱼ be their probabilities when the API call and result are supplied, p₀,ⱼ without a call, and pc,ⱼ with call text but no result. Use nonnegative future-token weights wⱼ. Define L+=−Σwⱼlog p₊,ⱼ and the two baseline losses similarly. Toolformer keeps the candidate when min(L₀,Lc)−L+≥τ.

Let B be the baseline with the smaller weighted negative log likelihood. Subtracting logs turns the filter into a weighted likelihood ratio:

Δ=LB−L+=∑jwjlog⁡p+,jpB,j=log⁡∏j(p+,jpB,j)wj,Keep if∏j(p+,jpB,j)wj≥eτ.\begin{aligned}\Delta&=\mathcal L_B-\mathcal L_+=\sum_jw_j\log\frac{p_{+,j}}{p_{B,j}}\\&=\log\prod_j\left(\frac{p_{+,j}}{p_{B,j}}\right)^{w_j},\\\text{Keep if}\quad\prod_j\left(\frac{p_{+,j}}{p_{B,j}}\right)^{w_j}&\ge e^\tau.\end{aligned}ΔKeep ifj∏​(pB,j​p+,j​​)wj​​=LB​−L+​=j∑​wj​logpB,j​p+,j​​=logj∏​(pB,j​p+,j​​)wj​,≥eτ.​

When weights are all one, this is a ratio of autoregressive probabilities for the scored continuation. With general weights it is a weighted product, not necessarily a normalized sequence probability. The no-result baseline is essential: useful wording in the proposed call can reveal the answer even if the external execution contributes nothing. The test demands improvement beyond the stronger of the two baselines.

This is an evidence criterion for training-data construction. It does not estimate task utility, API price, future state damage, or the benefit of a result many steps later. Teacher-forced probabilities of a known continuation are also different from the probability that free-running execution will solve a user task. To optimize that latter objective, one needs trajectory outcomes, calibrated value estimates, or another decision-relevant signal. The original method's filtering procedure and later finetuning are separate stages.

Exercise — Why the no-result baseline changes acceptance

For one scored future token with weight 1, probabilities are 0.2 without a call, 0.5 with call text alone, and 0.8 with the returned result. The threshold is τ=0.5 nats. Is the candidate retained? What would a filter using only the no-call baseline do?

Show worked solution
L0=−log⁡0.2≈1.609438,Lc=−log⁡0.5≈0.693147,L+=−log⁡0.8≈0.223144,Δ=min⁡(L0,Lc)−L+≈0.470004<0.5.\begin{aligned}\mathcal L_0&=-\log0.2\approx1.609438,\\\mathcal L_c&=-\log0.5\approx0.693147,\\\mathcal L_+&=-\log0.8\approx0.223144,\\\Delta&=\min(\mathcal L_0,\mathcal L_c)-\mathcal L_+\approx0.470004<0.5.\end{aligned}L0​Lc​L+​Δ​=−log0.2≈1.609438,=−log0.5≈0.693147,=−log0.8≈0.223144,=min(L0​,Lc​)−L+​≈0.470004<0.5.​

The specified filter rejects the call. Its returned information improves the stronger baseline by a factor 0.8/0.5=1.6, below exp(0.5)≈1.6487. A no-call-only filter gives log(0.8/0.2)=log4≈1.3863 and would accept, attributing to execution a benefit partly supplied by the call text itself.

What Toolformer does and does not solve

A calculator call is useful when a numeric result improves continuation likelihood. A calendar lookup may be essential for a task but have little effect on the probability of the surrounding prose. A tool with a delayed benefit several steps later may be poorly captured by a local loss reduction. Multi-call plans also create credit assignment: one lookup can be useful only because a later lookup uses its result. These limitations motivate trajectory-level supervision and RL.

Tool discovery and tool selection should also be distinguished. When thousands of APIs exist, the system may first retrieve a small set of relevant schemas, then choose a call. Errors can occur in schema retrieval, argument grounding, execution, or result interpretation. Function-calling benchmarks with a preselected handful of tools do not measure the full discovery problem. Report the available tool catalog and whether the correct tool was supplied by an oracle.

A practical tool contract includes types, units, allowed values, side effects, authentication scope, timeout semantics, error codes, and idempotency behavior. A natural-language description alone is often underspecified. “Price” might mean before or after tax; “date” might be local time or UTC; “update” might replace an object or patch selected fields. Models can learn interface conventions, but explicit contracts reduce ambiguity and make failures easier to diagnose.

5. 2023–2024: search over thoughts, actions, and executable candidates

Tree of Thoughts changes the unit of search

ToT treats a coherent partial solution as a node, rather than committing to one token-by-token continuation. A generator proposes candidate thoughts; an evaluator scores or votes on them; a search procedure such as breadth-first or depth-first search chooses which states to expand. The “thought” granularity is task-specific: an equation step, a plan, or a partial crossword assignment. [7]

The original figure contrasts direct input/output, one reasoning chain, multiple complete chains with majority vote, and a tree with intermediate evaluation. The distinction is where computation is allocated. Self-consistency spends on complete independent trajectories, while ToT can prune an unpromising partial trajectory and reuse a promising prefix. Green and red branches show selections and rejections, not ground-truth value functions magically available to the algorithm.

For Game of 24, a state can be the remaining numbers and operations used. The generator proposes an arithmetic operation; the evaluator estimates whether the remaining state can reach 24. This representation makes partial validity checkable and allows backtracking. A general research task has a much less precise state and value function, so the same search logic can be harder to apply. Search quality depends on the task representation as much as on the search algorithm.

Nleaves=O(bd)(branching b, depth d),Beam width k limits retained states but can discard the valid path,V^(s) allocates compute; terminal checks establish success,Ctotal≈Cproposal+Cvalue+Cenvironment+Ccontext.\begin{aligned}N_{\mathrm{leaves}}&=O(b^d)\quad\text{(branching }b\text{, depth }d\text{)},\\\text{Beam width }k&\text{ limits retained states but can discard the valid path},\\\hat V(s)&\text{ allocates compute; terminal checks establish success},\\C_{\mathrm{total}}&\approx C_{\mathrm{proposal}}+C_{\mathrm{value}}+C_{\mathrm{environment}}+C_{\mathrm{context}}.\end{aligned}Nleaves​Beam width kV^(s)Ctotal​​=O(bd)(branching b, depth d), limits retained states but can discard the valid path, allocates compute; terminal checks establish success,≈Cproposal​+Cvalue​+Cenvironment​+Ccontext​.​

The paper reports 74% Game-of-24 success for its strongest ToT setting versus 4% for the reported CoT setting with GPT-4. This demonstrates a large gain on a structured search task, with additional model calls and task-specific procedures. It does not imply a 70-point gain on arbitrary agent tasks, nor a comparison at equal token cost. A professional analysis asks how much of the gain comes from branching, evaluation, problem representation, and total compute.

LATS combines MCTS with real feedback

Language Agent Tree Search uses selection, expansion, evaluation, simulation, backpropagation, and reflection. A node contains the task and an action-observation history. Candidate actions are executed to obtain feedback; a value heuristic combines a language-model judgment with a self-consistency signal. Monte Carlo tree search allocates exploration using visit counts and estimated returns. [8]

UCT⁡(child)=V(child)+clog⁡N(parent)N(child),After return r:N←N+1,V←V+r−VN.LATS combines LM evaluation and repeated-action consistency.\begin{aligned}\operatorname{UCT}(\mathrm{child})&=V(\mathrm{child})+c\sqrt{\frac{\log N(\mathrm{parent})}{N(\mathrm{child})}},\\\text{After return }r:\quad N&\leftarrow N+1,\\V&\leftarrow V+\frac{r-V}N.\\&\text{LATS combines LM evaluation and repeated-action consistency.}\end{aligned}UCT(child)After return r:NV​=V(child)+cN(child)logN(parent)​​,←N+1,←V+Nr−V​.LATS combines LM evaluation and repeated-action consistency.​

Follow the six panels. Selection chooses an existing branch; expansion creates alternatives; evaluation estimates promise after observations; simulation reaches a terminal result; backpropagation updates values along the visited path; reflection converts a failed attempt into textual guidance. Backpropagation here updates search statistics, not neural-network weights. The reflection also changes context rather than performing gradient descent. Confusing these update types overstates what the method learns permanently.

The HotpotQA experiment uses a 100-question subset with correctness feedback available after an answer and up to 50 sampled trajectories. That oracle feedback is a strong assumption: a deployed assistant usually does not know whether an arbitrary factual answer is correct. In coding, LATS evaluates candidates on generated tests during search and reserves the actual benchmark tests for final scoring. These are different feedback regimes and should not be summarized under one unqualified “agent accuracy.”

Derivation: confidence bonuses explain exploration, with assumptions that LLM search can violate

Start with a simpler problem than tree search: each candidate action i produces independent, identically distributed rewards in [0,1] with fixed mean μᵢ. After nᵢ samples, its empirical mean is μ̂ᵢ. Hoeffding's inequality provides a one-sided confidence bound:

P(μi−μ^i≥ε)≤e−2niε2,e−2niε2=δ,μi≤μ^i+log⁡(1/δ)2niwith probability at least 1−δ for this bound.\begin{aligned}P(\mu_i-\hat\mu_i\ge\varepsilon)&\le e^{-2n_i\varepsilon^2},\\e^{-2n_i\varepsilon^2}&=\delta,\\\mu_i&\le\hat\mu_i+\sqrt{\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{2n_i}}\\&\text{with probability at least }1-\delta\text{ for this bound}.\end{aligned}P(μi​−μ^​i​≥ε)e−2ni​ε2μi​​≤e−2ni​ε2,=δ,≤μ^​i​+2ni​log(1/δ)​​with probability at least 1−δ for this bound.​

Choosing δ to shrink with total visits N produces a bonus proportional to √(log N/nᵢ). The numerator gradually encourages reconsideration as other actions are sampled; the denominator shrinks uncertainty about frequently tried actions. UCT applies this exploration idea recursively to search-tree children. Its tunable constant absorbs reward scale and exploration preference. Unvisited children require an explicit initialization rule because nᵢ=0 makes the formula undefined.

Scorei=Q^i+clog⁡Nni,Q^new=nQ^old+Rn+1=Q^old+R−Q^oldn+1.\begin{aligned}\mathrm{Score}_i&=\hat Q_i+c\sqrt{\frac{\log N}{n_i}},\\\hat Q_{\mathrm{new}}&=\frac{n\hat Q_{\mathrm{old}}+R}{n+1}=\hat Q_{\mathrm{old}}+\frac{R-\hat Q_{\mathrm{old}}}{n+1}.\end{aligned}Scorei​Q^​new​​=Q^​i​+cni​logN​​,=n+1nQ^​old​+R​=Q^​old​+n+1R−Q^​old​​.​

The mean update is exact arithmetic for observed returns; it does not update neural weights. A language agent often breaks the stationary-bandit assumptions: reflection changes prompts, the tree policy changes continuations, model judges are biased, and environment actions may be irreversible. Consequently, a UCT-shaped score is not by itself a guarantee of valid confidence intervals or convergence for that agent. Terminal execution feedback and well-defined reset semantics are needed to interpret search statistics.

A score above one is not a probability above one; it is an optimistic ranking index. Similarly, agreement among sampled thoughts is not an independent reward sample unless it is linked to actual task correctness. This distinction is especially important when a heuristic evaluator repeatedly validates its own mistaken premise.

Exercise — Choose a child without treating the score as a probability

A parent has N=100 visits. Child A has mean 0.7 and nA=25; B has mean 0.5 and nB=4. With c=0.5 and natural logs, compute both scores and select the next child. Explain the result.

Show worked solution
ScoreA=0.7+0.5log⁡10025≈0.91460,ScoreB=0.5+0.5log⁡1004≈1.03649.\begin{aligned}\mathrm{Score}_A&=0.7+0.5\sqrt{\frac{\log100}{25}}\approx0.91460,\\\mathrm{Score}_B&=0.5+0.5\sqrt{\frac{\log100}{4}}\approx1.03649.\end{aligned}ScoreA​ScoreB​​=0.7+0.525log100​​≈0.91460,=0.5+0.54log100​​≈1.03649.​

B is selected because its much smaller visit count yields a larger exploration bonus, despite a worse observed mean. The value 1.03649 is an index, not a calibrated success probability. If the underlying evaluator is systematically wrong, more exploration of its scores need not reveal the correct task solution.

Reversibility is a requirement, not an implementation convenience

Copying a text prefix recreates a reasoning state but does not undo a database write, purchase, or sent message. Search in a real environment needs snapshots, isolated sandboxes, a simulator, reversible actions, or a plan that delays irreversible effects. Otherwise, two candidate branches interact through shared state and the search tree no longer represents independent alternatives. This is why coding in isolated worktrees and browser tasks in resettable benchmark environments are natural search settings.

A weak evaluator can be exploited by increased search. If each candidate has a small probability of receiving a false-positive score, exploring many candidates increases the chance of finding one. The resulting best-scoring answer can be less trustworthy than a random candidate. Use independent final checks, hidden tests, or diverse evaluators when possible. The bottleneck often shifts from generating candidates to reliably selecting them.

Reflection and self-refinement are different from search

Self-refinement asks a model to critique and revise a candidate, often within one task. Reflexion stores verbal lessons from a failed attempt and includes them in subsequent attempts. Neither requires a parameter update. Their success depends on whether feedback diagnoses a real cause rather than narrating a plausible explanation after the fact. A model that did not observe the hidden failure reason can generate a confident but wrong lesson. [9]

The original diagram separates actor, evaluator, self-reflection module, short-term trajectory, and longer-term experience. The right-side algorithm repeats attempts until success or budget exhaustion. The evaluator's feedback is the crucial input to the reflection. The memory is useful when it changes a later decision, such as checking a precondition or avoiding a previously invalid API argument; merely appending generic advice increases context without supplying new information.

Compare reflection with a matched retry baseline. Both get additional attempts, so an improvement over one-shot generation does not isolate the value of reflection. Test retries with and without the stored lesson, preserve the same sampling budget, and evaluate on new tasks if claiming transferable learning. Within-task recovery, cross-task memory, and weight-level generalization are three different achievements.

6. 2023–2026: memory as a learned and managed information system

Four memory objects with different semantics

Working memory contains the current goal, recent observations, pending actions, and constraints. Episodic memory stores prior task trajectories or summarized events. Semantic memory stores facts and reusable abstractions. Procedural memory stores executable skills or action policies. An agent can use all four, but they require different retrieval and update rules. A failed API call is an episode; “this API uses UTC” is a semantic fact; a tested wrapper converting local time to UTC is a procedure.

Generative Agents couples an experience stream with retrieval based on relevance, recency, and importance, then produces higher-level reflections and plans. The contribution is an architecture for behavior conditioned on accumulated experience. Believable simulated behavior is its task, which differs from verified completion of a software or business workflow. Its memory scoring provides an influential design pattern, but its evaluation should not be transplanted to unrelated reliability claims. [11]

MemGPT: explicit control over a context hierarchy

MemGPT treats the model's finite context as a managed working area, backed by external recall and archival stores. The model can call functions to read or update memory, and control-flow mechanisms let it continue internal work before returning to the user. This resembles an operating-system abstraction: not every stored item must be resident in the current context, and movement between levels is explicit. [12]

The original figure distinguishes system instructions, writable working context, and a FIFO queue inside the finite context window. Recall storage holds interaction history; archival storage holds longer-lived external material. Function execution and the queue manager mediate movement. These are semantic memory tiers. They are not the same as HBM/DDR/SSD tiers for a model's KV cache, which store numerical attention state for a particular token prefix and model version.

The hierarchy introduces a replacement-policy problem. Evicting a recent observation is harmless only if the agent can retrieve it later or preserve its decision-relevant consequences. A summary can omit an exact filename, exception, or unresolved dependency that becomes important later. Store stable identifiers and provenance alongside summaries. Retrieval should return enough context to distinguish an old fact from a superseded one, and writing new memory should not silently erase conflicting evidence.

Derivation: a useful memory must preserve action-relevant distinctions

Let full history H be compressed into memory M=φ(H), and S denote the environment facts relevant to the task. Since M is a function of H, the variables form the information chain S→H→M. The data-processing inequality gives I(S;M)≤I(S;H). Compression cannot manufacture observations that were absent from the history.

Preserving all information is unnecessary if the task uses only a small part. A sufficient memory for future control would satisfy P(future observations,rewards|H,planned actions)=P(future observations,rewards|M,planned actions). This is a strong condition. A fluent summary can fail it by dropping which test suite ran, whether a write committed, or which document supplied a claim.

A local decision guarantee. Suppose the full-history belief is b and the compressed-memory belief is b̃, with TV(b,b̃)≤ε. For a final action d, let u(d,s)∈[0,1]. Then |E_bu(d,s)−E_b̃u(d,s)|≤ε. If d* maximizes true-belief utility and d̃ maximizes compressed-belief utility:

Ebu(d∗,s)−Ebu(d~,s)=[Ebu(d∗)−Eb~u(d∗)]+[Eb~u(d∗)−Eb~u(d~)]+[Eb~u(d~)−Ebu(d~)]≤2ε.\begin{aligned}\mathbb E_bu(d^*,s)-\mathbb E_bu(\tilde d,s)&=[\mathbb E_bu(d^*)-\mathbb E_{\tilde b}u(d^*)]\\&\quad+[\mathbb E_{\tilde b}u(d^*)-\mathbb E_{\tilde b}u(\tilde d)]\\&\quad+[\mathbb E_{\tilde b}u(\tilde d)-\mathbb E_bu(\tilde d)]\\&\le2\varepsilon.\end{aligned}Eb​u(d∗,s)−Eb​u(d~,s)​=[Eb​u(d∗)−Eb~​u(d∗)]+[Eb~​u(d∗)−Eb~​u(d~)]+[Eb~​u(d~)−Eb​u(d~)]≤2ε.​

The middle term is nonpositive by optimality under b̃. This establishes how a quantified belief error could control one decision's utility loss. It does not show that a summary has small ε, nor does it automatically bound every future adaptive decision. Evaluation should ask which distinctions were lost and whether they can change the action, not only whether the summary sounds complete.

Memory selection can also be modeled as a budget problem. Under an explicitly additive approximation, item i has probability pi of being needed, benefit vi when available, and token cost ci. Choose binary xi to maximize Σpivi xi subject to Σci xi≤B. This is a knapsack problem; ranking by benefit per token is not generally optimal for indivisible items. Real memories interact through redundancy, contradiction, and joint prerequisites, so even that objective is only a baseline.

Exercise — An indistinguishable summary and a misleading greedy policy

Two equally likely histories summarize to the same memory: in one, a remote update committed; in the other, it did not. The correct next action is different. What is the best accuracy of a deterministic decision based only on this memory? Separately, a token budget is 10 and candidate memory items have (cost,benefit) values (6,10), (5,8), (5,8). Compare greedy ratio selection with the optimum.

Show worked solution

The same memory forces the same deterministic action in both histories, so at most one of the two equally likely cases is handled correctly: accuracy≤0.5. Randomizing cannot improve the average without new information. A status read or retained transaction identifier can break the aliasing.

Benefit/cost ratios are 10/6≈1.667 and 8/5=1.6 for each other item. Greedy chooses the 6-token item, leaving 4 unused tokens and benefit 10. Selecting the two 5-token items uses the entire budget and yields 16. Ratio ranking is optimal for a fractional relaxation, but memory chunks here are indivisible.

Voyager: skills are executable memories

Voyager combines an automatic curriculum, iterative code generation with environment feedback, and a growing library of reusable skills in Minecraft. The curriculum selects tasks that expand the agent's capabilities; the code policy uses a programming interface; successful behaviors become callable library entries. This transforms prior experience into reusable computation, reducing the need to regenerate low-level behavior on every task. [10]

A skill needs a precondition, effect, parameter contract, and failure behavior. A function that worked once may depend on a particular inventory, terrain, or API version. Retrieval by a natural-language description alone can choose a superficially similar but inapplicable skill. In deployment, attach tests and versioning, track observed success by context, and prefer composition through explicit interfaces. Procedural memory is most valuable when it turns a long unreliable action sequence into a shorter validated abstraction.

A-MEM and ACE: organization and incremental updates

A-MEM uses structured notes and links among related memories, allowing new experiences to reorganize associations rather than simply append chronological text. This addresses retrieval across episodes, but semantic links remain model-generated hypotheses and may be wrong. A memory graph should preserve original evidence so that a derived association can be checked or revised. [13]

ACE treats context as an evolving playbook. A generator attempts tasks, a reflector diagnoses outcomes, and a curator integrates compact changes. Items have identifiers and metadata such as helpful/harmful counts; updates are localized rather than repeatedly rewriting one monolithic summary. The paper diagnoses context collapse, where successive summarization loses useful detail, and uses incremental updates with later refinement to preserve accumulated knowledge. [14]

The dashed feedback path and lower “delta context items” path are the essential parts of the figure. New experience produces a small set of changes, which the curator merges into the existing playbook. This is closer to maintaining a structured knowledge base than replacing a prompt wholesale. It also creates a new quality-control problem: an incorrect lesson can persist and affect many future tasks, so item provenance, conflict resolution, and rollback are necessary design choices.

Offline context adaptation and online adaptation must be evaluated separately. Offline adaptation can use a training split and freeze the resulting playbook for testing. Online adaptation updates after each test episode, so task order and what feedback is exposed affect later results. Report the order, reset policy, and whether correctness labels are available. A memory system that sees answers after each task has a different information budget from one learning only from natural execution feedback.

7. 2024: the interface becomes an algorithmic contribution

SWE-agent: reduce the cognitive burden of computer interaction

SWE-agent studies the agent–computer interface, or ACI, for repository-level software repair. A model must locate relevant code, inspect it, edit it, and interpret tests. A general shell permits all these actions, but its output and command conventions were designed for humans. SWE-agent provides compact search results, a bounded file viewer with line numbers, integrated edits, and immediate feedback. These choices change what the model observes and which actions are easy to express. [16]

The original example places the file observation beside the edit action. Line numbers bind the action to a concrete location, and the edit combines a multi-line change into one operation. The important design principle is state alignment: the model should see the exact version of the code it is about to modify, then receive a refreshed view after the change. Without this, it can apply a correct conceptual edit to stale line numbers or lose track of whether a prior edit succeeded.

The paper's ablations show why human-friendly interaction is not automatically model-friendly. An iterative search interface encourages repeated “next result” calls, sometimes exhausting the budget. Summarized search exposes the matches together and encourages query refinement. A full-file view can flood context; too small a window hides dependencies. An edit command with syntax checking can block a malformed patch before it triggers a cascade of repair attempts.

The original ablation table is a compact causal lesson. On the paper's SWE-bench Lite setup, the 100-line viewer scores 18.0%, compared with 14.3% for 30 lines and 12.7% for the full file. Summarized search reaches 18.0%, while iterative search reaches 12.0%. Removing the specialized edit interface gives 10.3%; edit-time linting improves the corresponding edit setting from 15.0% to 18.0%. These are historical GPT-4 Turbo results under this harness, not current limits on software agents.

The deeper insight is that an interface changes the policy's effective action space and observation distribution. A compact edit command lowers the number of generated tokens and chances for syntax error. A bounded viewer changes which evidence is salient. A linting guard changes the transition dynamics by rejecting some actions. Therefore, an ACI is part of the learning environment, and an interface ablation can be as informative as a larger-model comparison.

Agentless: a structured pipeline is a serious baseline

Agentless decomposes repair into hierarchical localization, patch generation, and validation. It narrows from repository structure to files, then classes/functions, then edit locations. Multiple candidate patches are generated in a search/replace format. Reproduction and regression tests filter candidates, and normalized patches support selection. This is deliberate task-specific structure rather than an unrestricted action loop. [17]

Read the original pipeline from coarse localization across the top to patch generation and testing along the bottom. Each stage reduces a different uncertainty: where the issue lives, what change might repair it, whether the change addresses the issue, and whether existing behavior remains intact. The stage boundaries make ablations and cost accounting easier. They also restrict adaptability if an issue requires an unusual investigation outside the predefined sequence.

In the downloaded revised paper, Table 1 reports 96/300 resolved SWE-bench Lite tasks, or 32.0%, at an average reported cost of $0.70 using GPT-4o. The implementation samples multiple edit locations, patches, and reproduction tests; “agentless” does not mean one model call or zero search. The comparison establishes that a well-engineered pipeline can be competitive with general agents. It does not establish superiority at a common model version, cost budget, and environment for every baseline in that table.

CodeAct and OpenHands: executable code as a compositional action space

CodeAct represents actions as executable code, allowing variables, loops, conditions, and tool composition within one generated action. A code action can express a batch of dependent calculations more compactly than many separate natural-language tool calls. The execution environment returns concrete errors and values. The tradeoff is that a more expressive action space also permits larger mistakes, so sandboxing, resource limits, and observable effects matter. [36]

OpenHands provides a broader platform for software-agent execution, with runtimes, event streams, tools, and evaluation support. Infrastructure that records actions and observations consistently enables replay, inspection, and comparison across policies. Its contribution should be distinguished from a claim that one default agent algorithm is always best. A platform supplies the experimental substrate; a policy, prompt, model, and budget still define the evaluated system. [18]

Browser and GUI agents: perception errors become control errors

WebArena moves evaluation into realistic, resettable web applications with functional task checks. OSWorld extends this to real desktop applications and execution-based evaluation. These environments expose issues absent from static question answering: login state, navigation, hidden controls, asynchronous updates, cross-application workflows, and the need to verify saved artifacts. [26] [27]

A browser agent may act on a DOM or accessibility representation, screenshots, or both. Structured representations make element identity easier but may omit visual context; screenshots preserve appearance but require grounding a desired action to coordinates. A GUI action is only meaningful relative to a particular observation, viewport, scale, and application state. After scrolling or opening a dialog, previously inferred coordinates may be invalid.

UI-TARS develops a native screenshot-to-action model, combining perception, action prediction, reasoning, and iterative interaction training. The research direction shifts some work from a hand-designed wrapper into a learned visual policy. Yet the execution loop still needs post-action observation, timing, and completion checks. Better grounding cannot compensate for an incorrect high-level goal, and better planning cannot compensate for clicking the wrong object. Evaluate perception/grounding separately from long-horizon completion to locate the bottleneck. [37]

8. 2023–2026: what exactly is being optimized?

Four systems can all be called “self-improving agents” while updating entirely different objects. Context adaptation changes information provided to a fixed model. Program optimization changes prompts, demonstrations, or control flow. Policy learning changes model weights. Routing changes which model or tool receives a subtask. These updates have different data requirements, cost, generalization, and rollback properties.

Update targetExamplesTraining signalPersistent artifact
Context / memoryReflexion, A-MEM, ACEExecution feedback and curated lessonsNotes, playbooks, links, skill records
Prompts / programDSPy, TextGrad, ADASValidation metric, textual feedback, program evaluationInstructions, demonstrations, modules, control flow
Policy weightsToolformer, Search-R1, UI-TARS, Agent LightningSupervised trajectories or RL rewardsModel/adapters and training state
Resource selectionToolOrchestra, SkillOrchestraSuccess, latency, cost, competence estimatesOrchestrator policy or skill/agent statistics

DSPy: compile a declarative language-model program

DSPy separates the program's input/output signatures and composition from the exact prompt text or demonstrations used by each module. A module can request reasoning, retrieval, or prediction through a declared interface. An optimizer runs the program on examples, evaluates the outputs, and selects or constructs instructions and demonstrations that improve a metric. Successful intermediate traces can be bootstrapped as demonstrations for modules that lack directly labeled intermediate targets. [19]

This is a form of program-level credit allocation through evaluation, not ordinary backpropagation through a frozen black-box API. A downstream metric can select a useful upstream retrieval query even when no human wrote the ideal query. But if the metric rewards a shortcut, the compiler will optimize that shortcut. A held-out validation set is therefore as important as in conventional machine learning, and the final test set must remain outside optimizer selection.

The main benefit is portability and systematic optimization. A hand-written prompt often encodes assumptions about one model's formatting and reasoning style. Recompiling a modular program against a new model can adapt those details while preserving the high-level task structure. The high-level structure still matters: a program that retrieves only once cannot discover a missing second-hop fact unless its control flow permits another retrieval.

TextGrad and ADAS optimize at different abstraction levels

TextGrad propagates natural-language feedback through a computation graph. A critic describes how an intermediate variable could change to improve an objective, and an optimizer uses that feedback to revise text or other editable components. The gradient metaphor is useful for organizing credit, but the feedback is not a mathematically exact derivative. It can be noisy, inconsistent, or based on a mistaken diagnosis. [20]

ADAS searches over agent designs expressed as code, using evaluated candidates and an archive of prior designs to propose new ones. This expands optimization beyond wording into control structure. It also increases the risk of overfitting a benchmark through repeated program search. Separate design-search examples, validation examples, and final test tasks, and count the search budget when claiming efficiency. A cheap deployed program may have required an expensive discovery process. [21]

Search-R1: learn the search-and-reason loop with outcome rewards

Search-R1 trains a model to generate queries and interleave retrieved evidence with reasoning through RL. Search results are inserted as observations; the model continues generating its own tokens afterward. A crucial implementation detail is retrieved-token masking: external text is not sampled from the policy and should not receive policy-gradient credit as though the model had generated it. [38]

A trajectory probability factors over policy-generated actions, while environment transitions and tool results come from other distributions. If a retrieved sentence is included in the policy loss, the model is rewarded for reproducing an observation it did not choose. Correct masking preserves the distinction between action and evidence. The final reward can teach useful query behavior indirectly, but sparse success signals make long multi-step credit assignment difficult.

The reported gains are measured on specified question-answering datasets and retriever/corpus configurations. Transfer to unrestricted web research is a separate problem: pages change, search costs vary, documents can be adversarial, and there may be no exact answer string. Training an effective retrieval policy requires matching the training environment to the information access and feedback available at deployment.

Agent Lightning: separate agent execution from policy training

Agent Lightning defines a unified transition interface around model calls, allowing application code and tool execution to remain separate from the RL trainer. A transition records the input context, generated output, and reward information. Complex agent control flow is converted into a sequence of trainable decisions rather than requiring every framework to concatenate all interactions into one enormous token sequence. [22]

The original figure compares single-call GRPO, concatenated multi-turn trajectories, and transition-based LightningRL. In the right panel, separate model calls retain their own input contexts and generated outputs. A credit-assignment component distributes episode feedback over those actions before token-level learning. This makes integration modular, but it does not solve credit assignment automatically. The paper's basic implementation can assign the same episode reward to transitions; more precise action values remain a research problem.

The architecture also separates GPU-heavy generation/training from diverse application runtimes. Many tool environments can run concurrently while a serving backend batches model calls. This creates systems questions: how to identify the policy version of each action, how to handle long-running tools, how to reset environment state, and how to prevent one rollout's mutations leaking into another. A transition dataset without provenance is insufficient to reproduce the update.

For multiple trainable models, optimizing each independently treats the others as part of a changing environment. This nonstationarity can undermine coordination. A shared team reward also makes it hard to identify which model helped or harmed the outcome. Multi-agent RL methods, centralized critics, counterfactual credit, or carefully staged training may help, but none is implied merely by recording a multi-agent trace.

Derivation: assign learning credit only to decisions the policy actually sampled

Let a trajectory τ contain the agent's sampled decisions aₜ, tool observations oₜ, and terminal reward R. Assume the environment and tool distributions do not depend on the trained parameter θ. The trajectory density factors into initial/environment terms and policy terms πθ(aₜ|hₜ). The likelihood-ratio identity gives:

J(θ)=Eτ∼pθ[R(τ)],∇θJ=∫pθ(τ)R(τ)∇θlog⁡pθ(τ) dτ=E ⁣[R∑t∇θlog⁡πθ(at∣ht)].\begin{aligned}J(\theta)&=\mathbb E_{\tau\sim p_\theta}[R(\tau)],\\\nabla_\theta J&=\int p_\theta(\tau)R(\tau)\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(\tau)\,d\tau\\&=\mathbb E\!\left[R\sum_t\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a_t\mid h_t)\right].\end{aligned}J(θ)∇θ​J​=Eτ∼pθ​​[R(τ)],=∫pθ​(τ)R(τ)∇θ​logpθ​(τ)dτ=E[Rt∑​∇θ​logπθ​(at​∣ht​)].​

This moves differentiation from the possibly nondifferentiable tool execution into the probability of the agent's choices. Past rewards can be removed from a decision's weight under the causal sampling assumptions, producing reward-to-go. Any baseline b(hₜ) independent of the sampled action can be subtracted without changing the expected gradient:

Ea∼π[b(h)∇log⁡π(a∣h)]=b(h)∑aπ(a∣h)∇log⁡π(a∣h)=b(h)∇∑aπ(a∣h)=b(h)∇1=0.\begin{aligned}\mathbb E_{a\sim\pi}[b(h)\nabla\log\pi(a\mid h)]&=b(h)\sum_a\pi(a\mid h)\nabla\log\pi(a\mid h)\\&=b(h)\nabla\sum_a\pi(a\mid h)=b(h)\nabla1=0.\end{aligned}Ea∼π​[b(h)∇logπ(a∣h)]​=b(h)a∑​π(a∣h)∇logπ(a∣h)=b(h)∇a∑​π(a∣h)=b(h)∇1=0.​

Thus an imperfect value baseline can reduce variance without biasing this on-policy identity, provided its use and gradients are handled correctly. The baseline is normally treated as fixed in the actor gradient. Off-policy trajectories require additional correction or a deliberately changed surrogate; merely recording an old tool trace does not make it an on-policy sample.

Variance-optimal scalar baseline for one score vector. Let g=∇logπ(a|h). Minimizing E[(R−b)²∥g∥²|h] over b yields b*=E[R∥g∥²|h]/E[∥g∥²|h], by differentiating the quadratic. A plain expected-return baseline is common and useful, but is not always the exact variance minimizer because score magnitudes can correlate with rewards.

For an LLM agent, generated reasoning/action tokens are policy decisions; returned web text, execution output, and user messages are environment observations. Their token likelihoods must not be included as if the policy generated them in the same policy-gradient term. They can still influence later action probabilities as conditioning context. If a jointly trained delegate or simulator also depends on θ, its dependence must be modeled explicitly. This is why actor provenance, policy versions, and masks are algorithmic requirements in Search-R1 and Agent Lightning, rather than bookkeeping details.

9. Multi-agent systems: division of labor is a hypothesis to test

Conversation, role structure, and independent evidence

AutoGen provides programmable conversations among agents that can use tools and involve humans. MetaGPT structures collaboration around roles, standardized procedures, and intermediate artifacts. Multiagent debate has agents propose and critique answers over several rounds. These approaches differ in what communication is intended to accomplish: execute a workflow, enforce task decomposition, or challenge competing hypotheses. [15] [39] [40]

Distinct role prompts do not guarantee distinct knowledge or independent errors. Several instances of the same model may share the same blind spot, and early persuasive messages can cause later agents to converge prematurely. Diversity can come from different evidence sources, tools, models, search strategies, or independently generated solutions. For factual tasks, independent retrieval plus source verification often supplies more meaningful diversity than assigning theatrical job titles.

A good delegation contract specifies the subproblem, available inputs, required output artifact, assumptions, constraints, and completion test. It also defines ownership of shared state. Two agents editing the same file without coordination can overwrite one another even if both are individually competent. A manager should integrate evidence and artifacts, not merely concatenate reports. Contradictions need resolution against sources or execution results.

When parallelism is useful

Independent literature searches, disjoint code modules, alternative proofs, and separate experiment analyses can benefit from parallel work. A task whose next step depends tightly on the previous observation offers less parallelism. Every subagent also pays initialization and context costs, and the parent pays integration cost. More workers may lower latency while increasing total tokens, or increase both if coordination dominates.

Tcompletion≈Tserial planning+max⁡iTsubtask,i+Tintegration+Tverification,Ccompute=Cparent+∑iCworker,i+Ccommunication,Vcommunication=O(n2m)per all-to-all round,for n agents and length-m messages, before repeated-context effects.\begin{aligned}T_{\mathrm{completion}}&\approx T_{\mathrm{serial\ planning}}+\max_iT_{\mathrm{subtask},i}\\&\quad+T_{\mathrm{integration}}+T_{\mathrm{verification}},\\C_{\mathrm{compute}}&=C_{\mathrm{parent}}+\sum_iC_{\mathrm{worker},i}+C_{\mathrm{communication}},\\V_{\mathrm{communication}}&=O(n^2m)\quad\text{per all-to-all round},\\&\text{for }n\text{ agents and length-}m\text{ messages, before repeated-context effects}.\end{aligned}Tcompletion​Ccompute​Vcommunication​​≈Tserial planning​+imax​Tsubtask,i​+Tintegration​+Tverification​,=Cparent​+i∑​Cworker,i​+Ccommunication​,=O(n2m)per all-to-all round,for n agents and length-m messages, before repeated-context effects.​

These equations are design models, not empirical scaling laws. They show why a sparse communication graph, shared artifacts, and bounded reports can be more efficient than an all-to-all chat. They also show why reporting only wall time hides total cost. Evaluate success, latency, tokens, tool calls, and integration failures together.

Derivation: ten agents can provide far less than ten independent opinions

Let Xi indicate whether agent i is correct on a task, with common success probability p and variance p(1−p). Suppose every pair has correlation ρ. For the average correctness X̄ over m agents:

Var⁡(Xˉ)=1m2[∑iVar⁡(Xi)+∑i≠jCov⁡(Xi,Xj)]=p(1−p)m[1+(m−1)ρ],meff=m1+(m−1)ρ.\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)&=\frac1{m^2}\left[\sum_i\operatorname{Var}(X_i)+\sum_{i\ne j}\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j)\right]\\&=\frac{p(1-p)}m[1+(m-1)\rho],\\m_{\mathrm{eff}}&=\frac m{1+(m-1)\rho}.\end{aligned}Var(Xˉ)meff​​=m21​​i∑​Var(Xi​)+i=j∑​Cov(Xi​,Xj​)​=mp(1−p)​[1+(m−1)ρ],=1+(m−1)ρm​.​

At ρ=0, variance falls as 1/m. At ρ=1, every agent repeats the same success or failure and there is no variance reduction. For ρ>0, meff approaches 1/ρ as m grows. This calculation is about the average under an exchangeable equal-correlation model. It does not uniquely determine majority-vote accuracy; different joint error distributions can have the same pairwise correlations and different tail probabilities.

Independent evidence can be more valuable than independent wording. Different source retrieval, different tests, and independently executed constraints can change the error dependence. Merely assigning different personas to the same model and context need not do so. Shared hidden assumptions are especially dangerous when the agents also evaluate one another.

A verifier is another conditional model. If candidate correctness has prior p, the verifier accepts a correct candidate with rate t and an incorrect one with rate f, Bayes' rule gives:

P(correct∣accepted)=ptpt+(1−p)f,P(accepted)=pt+(1−p)f.\begin{aligned}P(\mathrm{correct}\mid\mathrm{accepted})&=\frac{pt}{pt+(1-p)f},\\P(\mathrm{accepted})&=pt+(1-p)f.\end{aligned}P(correct∣accepted)P(accepted)​=pt+(1−p)fpt​,=pt+(1−p)f.​

High acceptance is not high precision. A rare-correctness regime can yield many false approvals even with a modest false-positive rate. Searching more candidates increases the chance of finding a correct solution, but can also expose a weak verifier to more chances for false acceptance. Candidate generation, verification, and final selection must be evaluated jointly.

Exercise — Count independent evidence and calibrate acceptance

Ten agents have common p=0.8 and pairwise correlation ρ=0.3. Calculate meff and Var(X̄). For a separate candidate generator with correctness p=0.4, a verifier has t=0.9 and f=0.1. What is accepted-answer precision?

Show worked solution
meff=101+9×0.3=103.7≈2.703,Var⁡(Xˉ)=0.8×0.2×3.710=0.0592,Var⁡independent=0.1610=0.016,Verifier precision=0.4×0.90.4×0.9+0.6×0.1=0.360.42≈0.8571.\begin{aligned}m_{\mathrm{eff}}&=\frac{10}{1+9\times0.3}=\frac{10}{3.7}\approx2.703,\\\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)&=\frac{0.8\times0.2\times3.7}{10}=0.0592,\\\operatorname{Var}_{\mathrm{independent}}&=\frac{0.16}{10}=0.016,\\\text{Verifier precision}&=\frac{0.4\times0.9}{0.4\times0.9+0.6\times0.1}\\&=\frac{0.36}{0.42}\approx0.8571.\end{aligned}meff​Var(Xˉ)Varindependent​Verifier precision​=1+9×0.310​=3.710​≈2.703,=100.8×0.2×3.7​=0.0592,=100.16​=0.016,=0.4×0.9+0.6×0.10.4×0.9​=0.420.36​≈0.8571.​

The ten correlated agents reduce variance about as much as 2.7 independent agents in this model. The verifier accepts 42% of candidates, but roughly 14.3% of accepted candidates are still wrong. Neither an effective-count calculation nor an acceptance rate certifies a particular final answer.

Debate versus verification

A debate may expose a mistaken premise, but agreement at the end is not a correctness certificate. If a verifier can execute a proof checker, unit test, or exact query, that evidence should outrank rhetorical confidence. If no strong verifier exists, maintain the provenance of competing claims and measure calibration rather than forcing premature consensus. Compare debate with independent sampling plus a selector at the same call budget to identify what communication adds.

The most informative ablations remove one communication edge or role at a time, freeze tool access, and measure the resulting change. If removing a critic improves performance, investigate whether it was introducing false objections or consuming the budget. If a manager always rewrites correct worker outputs into incorrect ones, the integration policy is the bottleneck. The system should be decomposed into measurable decisions rather than described as an undifferentiated “team.”

10. 2025–2026: learn which model or tool should do the work

ToolOrchestra: a small controller can coordinate expensive capabilities

ToolOrchestra trains an 8B orchestrator to choose among basic tools, specialized models, and generalist models. Its reward combines correctness, efficiency, and user preferences. The tool catalog and pricing configurations vary during training so that the policy can learn conditional resource allocation rather than one fixed preference for a particular model. [23]

The original figure places ordinary APIs and language models in the same callable toolbox. The orchestrator alternates reasoning and calls, receives responses, and eventually answers. The lower reward loop explicitly includes outcome, efficiency, and preference. The 8B size describes the controller, not all computation used to solve a task. If it calls a much larger frontier model, that model's capability and cost are part of the system.

A central design issue is the reward's exchange rate. How much accuracy is worth a dollar or a minute? ToolOrchestra constructs normalized trajectory features and preference weights, with unsuccessful trajectories treated separately. Batch normalization of costs or rewards can change incentives when the candidate distribution changes. A deployment should evaluate the resulting quality-cost frontier under actual prices and latency, not assume training reward units remain calibrated forever.

The original Table 1 is more informative than the headline. On the paper's text-only HLE evaluation, Orchestrator-8B scores 37.1 versus 35.1 for its GPT-5 baseline with basic tools. The reported mean cost across HLE and FRAMES is 9.2 versus 30.2 US cents, and mean latency is 8.2 versus 19.8 minutes. The table also includes a separately reported GPT-5 full-HLE result; that row uses a different subset and must not be treated as the same experiment. Tool availability, model endpoints, and prices are part of the result.

SkillOrchestra: make competence conditional on the required skill

SkillOrchestra represents reusable skills and estimates agent-specific competence and cost for those skills from execution experience. Routing can then condition on the active skill requirements of a subtask. This differs from assigning one global quality score to each model or learning an opaque route directly from every full task. It is a way to make transfer and resource choice more interpretable. [24]

An explanatory routing objective is to choose the agent with the best estimated skill-weighted competence minus a cost penalty. The estimates need calibration and uncertainty: an untested agent may appear cheap but have unknown success probability, while a model excellent at arithmetic may be poor at locating a current fact. The skill taxonomy itself can be wrong or too coarse. Evaluate whether learned competence transfers to new task compositions and whether routing adapts when tool costs or capabilities change.

Routing also includes escalation and stopping. A cheap model can attempt a bounded subproblem, and a stronger model can be called if the evidence suggests uncertainty or failure. But confidence must be externally calibrated; a weaker model can be confidently wrong. The value of escalation depends on the stronger model's conditional success on the cases the router sends it, not only its average benchmark score.

Derivation: cost-aware routing is a constrained optimization problem

For task x, let qi(x) be the calibrated probability or expected utility of success using option i, and ci(x) its expected resource cost. Let ρi(x) be a routing probability. A one-shot router with average budget B solves:

max⁡ρ  Ex∑iρi(x)qi(x)subject toEx∑iρi(x)ci(x)≤B,ρi(x)≥0,∑iρi(x)=1.\begin{aligned}\max_\rho\;&\mathbb E_x\sum_i\rho_i(x)q_i(x)\\\text{subject to}\quad&\mathbb E_x\sum_i\rho_i(x)c_i(x)\le B,\\&\rho_i(x)\ge0,\quad\sum_i\rho_i(x)=1.\end{aligned}ρmax​subject to​Ex​i∑​ρi​(x)qi​(x)Ex​i∑​ρi​(x)ci​(x)≤B,ρi​(x)≥0,i∑​ρi​(x)=1.​

Introduce a nonnegative multiplier λ for the cost constraint. The Lagrangian is E_xΣᵢρi(x)[qi(x)−λci(x)]+λB. For fixed λ, each task independently chooses the largest adjusted score qi−λci, with randomization permitted at ties. Increasing λ puts a larger penalty on expensive calls. Under the finite/convex randomized formulation and feasible budgets, this gives the supporting quality-cost tradeoff; choosing λ still requires satisfying the actual budget.

Prefer B to A ifqB−qA>λ(cB−cA),λ∗=qB−qAcB−cA,cB>cA.\begin{aligned}\text{Prefer }B\text{ to }A\text{ if}\quad q_B-q_A&>\lambda(c_B-c_A),\\\lambda^*&=\frac{q_B-q_A}{c_B-c_A},\quad c_B>c_A.\end{aligned}Prefer B to A ifqB​−qA​λ∗​>λ(cB​−cA​),=cB​−cA​qB​−qA​​,cB​>cA​.​

This makes the quality-cost exchange rate explicit. More expensive models should be selected for tasks where their conditional advantage justifies the additional cost, not merely because they have a higher overall benchmark average. A skill-conditioned router estimates qi from task-relevant competence; model endpoints, prices, and failure distributions can change those estimates.

Multi-step orchestration is harder than this one-shot baseline. A cheap first call may reveal whether escalation is worthwhile. The gain from escalation is conditional on that new evidence, and must include the cost of deciding which answer to trust. Likewise, latency and price are separate constraints unless a justified utility function combines them. ToolOrchestra's learned trajectory reward is one implementation choice within this broader sequential allocation problem.

Exercise — Find a routing threshold and a budget-feasible mixture

On identical tasks, model A has success 0.7 at cost 1 and B has success 0.9 at cost 4. Which is chosen for λ=0.05 and λ=0.10? If average budget is 2.5, what randomized mixture maximizes success in this two-option model?

Show worked solution
λ=0.05:SA=0.70−0.05=0.65,SB=0.90−0.20=0.70⇒B,λ=0.10:SA=0.60,SB=0.50⇒A,λ∗=0.9−0.74−1=115≈0.06667.\begin{aligned}\lambda=0.05:\quad S_A&=0.70-0.05=0.65,&S_B&=0.90-0.20=0.70\quad\Rightarrow B,\\\lambda=0.10:\quad S_A&=0.60,&S_B&=0.50\quad\Rightarrow A,\\\lambda^*&=\frac{0.9-0.7}{4-1}=\frac1{15}\approx0.06667.\end{aligned}λ=0.05:SA​λ=0.10:SA​λ∗​=0.70−0.05=0.65,=0.60,=4−10.9−0.7​=151​≈0.06667.​SB​SB​​=0.90−0.20=0.70⇒B,=0.50⇒A,​

Let z be the fraction sent to B. Expected cost is 1(1−z)+4z=1+3z≤2.5, so z≤0.5. Since B improves success, use z=0.5. Expected success is 0.7(0.5)+0.9(0.5)=0.8. This assumes calibrated utilities and identical tasks. With task heterogeneity, prioritize B on cases with larger conditional gain per added cost.

11. Evaluation evolves from answers to stateful reliability

The benchmark defines the problem the agent is solving

SWE-bench asks for patches that resolve real repository issues under tests. WebArena checks outcomes in web applications. OSWorld checks desktop workflows. GAIA combines information gathering, reasoning, and tool use for assistant-style questions. τ-bench introduces user dialogue, policy constraints, database APIs, and repeat reliability. τ²-Bench adds dual control: both the user and agent can change parts of the environment. [25] [26] [27] [30] [28] [29]

A benchmark score is inseparable from its observation interface, action space, environment version, reset procedure, tool permissions, budget, and success detector. A model with access to hidden tests is solving a different problem from one using generated tests. A browser agent with a full DOM and one with screenshots alone have different information. An oracle answer checker during search changes the difficulty dramatically.

τ²-Bench: coordination requires reasoning about another actor

In the original diagram, the agent controls domain APIs while the user controls device-side actions. Both influence the shared world. The agent may need to instruct the user to change a phone setting, then infer whether the change occurred from a message and subsequent observations. A correct backend action alone cannot complete every task.
