This makes instruction clarity, diagnosis, and coordinated state tracking part of the benchmark rather than treating the user as a static source of prompts.

User simulators introduce their own measurement questions. A simulator may misunderstand an instruction, reveal information unrealistically, or act with a consistency different from real users. Report the simulator model and prompting policy, and analyze failures attributable to the user simulation separately from agent mistakes. The benchmark remains useful, but a simulated interaction success rate is not automatically a real-customer success rate.

pass@k and pass^k ask opposite questions

pass@k measures whether at least one of k attempts succeeds. It is useful for candidate generation when a selector can identify the successful output. pass^k measures whether all k attempts succeed, emphasizing repeat reliability. Under an illustrative independent success probability p, the former is 1−(1−p)^k and the latter is p^k. They diverge quickly.

p=0.8,k=8,P(at least one success)=1−0.28=99.999744%,P(all eight succeed)=0.88=16.777216%,P(end-to-end success)≈qnfor n mandatory steps, independent unrecovered failures.\begin{aligned}p&=0.8,\quad k=8,\\P(\text{at least one success})&=1-0.2^8=99.999744\%,\\P(\text{all eight succeed})&=0.8^8=16.777216\%,\\P(\text{end-to-end success})&\approx q^n\\&\text{for }n\text{ mandatory steps, independent unrecovered failures}.\end{aligned}pP(at least one success)P(all eight succeed)P(end-to-end success)​=0.8,k=8,=1−0.28=99.999744%,=0.88=16.777216%,≈qnfor n mandatory steps, independent unrecovered failures.​

The original τ-bench figure plots rising dotted pass@k curves and falling solid pass^k curves for the same historical model family. The gap reveals how a system can look excellent when allowed many attempts while remaining unreliable on repeated real tasks. In the paper's retail setting, even the strongest evaluated agent's pass^8 falls below 25%. These are 2024 results, not a claim about current models, and the chart averages over heterogeneous task difficulties rather than assuming one common p.

Illustrative independent-event model. Retries need a reliable success detector; repeated mutations may require idempotency and recovery.

For finite repeated trials, unbiased pass@k estimators often use the number of observed successes c among n samples: 1−choose(n−c,k)/choose(n,k). A corresponding all-success estimate uses choose(c,k)/choose(n,k). Independence, identical conditions, and task heterogeneity still matter. Retries after observing prior failures are adaptive attempts, so they are not the same experiment as independent samples from a fixed policy.

Derivation: repeated success, candidate success, and task heterogeneity

For one fixed task with independent attempts of success probability p, all k attempts succeed with probability pᵏ. At least one succeeds with probability 1−(1−p)ᵏ, obtained by subtracting the probability that all fail. The first measures repeat reliability; the second measures candidate coverage when a valid selection mechanism can identify success.

Benchmarks contain tasks with different probabilities pj. Averaging over tasks gives E[pjᵏ] and E[1−(1−pj)ᵏ]. These are not generally obtained by inserting the average p̄. For k≥2, xᵏ is convex and 1−(1−x)ᵏ is concave, so Jensen gives:

Mean passk=E[pjk]≥(E[pj])k,Mean pass@k=E[1−(1−pj)k]≤1−(1−E[pj])k.\begin{aligned}\mathrm{Mean\ pass}^{k}&=\mathbb E[p_j^k]\ge(\mathbb E[p_j])^k,\\\mathrm{Mean\ pass@}k&=\mathbb E[1-(1-p_j)^k]\le1-(1-\mathbb E[p_j])^k.\end{aligned}Mean passkMean pass@k​=E[pjk​]≥(E[pj​])k,=E[1−(1−pj​)k]≤1−(1−E[pj​])k.​

If half the tasks always succeed and half always fail, average pass@1 is 0.5. Both repeat metrics remain 0.5 for every k. Plugging p̄=0.5 into the homogeneous formulas instead predicts pass^8≈0.00391 and pass@8≈0.99609. Repetition does not solve the always-failing half. This is why a benchmark's task-wise distribution and recurring failure modes matter.

Finite-sample estimation. Given n exchangeable independent attempts on one task, of which c succeed, imagine uniformly selecting a subset of k distinct attempts. There are choose(n,k) subsets; choose(n−c,k) contain only failures and choose(c,k) contain only successes. Thus:

pass@k^=1−(n−ck)(nk),passk^=(ck)(nk),k≤n.\begin{aligned}\widehat{\mathrm{pass@}k}&=1-\frac{\binom{n-c}{k}}{\binom nk},\\\widehat{\mathrm{pass}^{k}}&=\frac{\binom ck}{\binom nk},\quad k\le n.\end{aligned}pass@k​passk​​=1−(kn​)(kn−c​)​,=(kn​)(kc​)​,k≤n.​

Taking expectations under independent Bernoulli attempts yields the desired fixed-task probabilities, so these are unbiased estimators in that model. They differ from raising c/n to a power. Adaptive retries after reflection, changing tool availability, or partial environment mutations are different experiments; their attempts are not exchangeable draws from one fixed policy. Also, candidate coverage is only operationally useful when the agent can select or verify the successful candidate without an oracle.

Exercise — Use the finite-sample estimators

A fixed policy succeeds in c=7 of n=10 independent attempts on one task. Estimate pass@3 and pass^3 using subset counting. Compare with plugging p̂=0.7 into the population formulas, and explain why the answers differ.

Show worked solution
(103)=120,(33)=1,(73)=35,pass@3^=1−1120=119120≈0.991667,pass3^=35120≈0.291667,Plug-in pass@3=1−0.33=0.973,Plug-in pass3=0.73=0.343.\begin{aligned}\binom{10}3&=120,\quad\binom33=1,\quad\binom73=35,\\\widehat{\mathrm{pass@}3}&=1-\frac1{120}=\frac{119}{120}\approx0.991667,\\\widehat{\mathrm{pass}^{3}}&=\frac{35}{120}\approx0.291667,\\\mathrm{Plug\text{-}in\ pass@}3&=1-0.3^3=0.973,\\\mathrm{Plug\text{-}in\ pass}^{3}&=0.7^3=0.343.\end{aligned}(310​)pass@3​pass3​Plug-in pass@3Plug-in pass3​=120,(33​)=1,(37​)=35,=1−1201​=120119​≈0.991667,=12035​≈0.291667,=1−0.33=0.973,=0.73=0.343.​

The subset estimators count distinct observed attempts without replacement and are unbiased after averaging over repeated datasets under the iid model. The plug-in formulas apply a nonlinear transformation to an estimated p, which creates finite-sample bias. Neither estimate removes uncertainty from having only ten observations, and neither supports treating a changed retry policy as the same experiment.

Reliability includes the ability to detect and recover from failure

End-to-end reliability can improve by reducing error probability, detecting errors, or recovering before they propagate. A system with a modest first-attempt score and strong verification/recovery may be more useful than one with higher first-attempt accuracy but undetectable failures. Measure false success declarations, recovery success, duplicate actions, and residual state corruption, not only final task reward.

A timeout illustrates why recovery is a systems problem. An API request may have committed before the connection dropped. Blind retry can duplicate the mutation. An idempotency key, operation identifier, or fresh status read can distinguish safe retry from reconciliation. The agent's policy should have access to these signals, and the environment should expose errors in a machine-interpretable way. Better language reasoning cannot infer information that the interface never provides.

12. Security, evidence, and durable execution are part of competence

Retrieved documents, repository files, web pages, emails, and tool responses are data from the environment. They can contain instructions that conflict with the user's goal or tool permissions. AgentDojo and InjecAgent study indirect prompt injection through such content. This is especially relevant for agents because language from an untrusted source can influence a policy that has real action capabilities. [32] [33]

The central boundary is between evidence and authority. A document can supply a shipping address or explain an API; it should not silently acquire the right to change the task, reveal unrelated secrets, or authorize another tool action. Attach provenance and trust scope to content, constrain tools by least necessary capability, and evaluate defenses with both attack success and legitimate task utility. A defense that blocks every tool call prevents attacks by abandoning the task.

Durable execution also requires event records. Store a stable tool-call ID, arguments, start/end status, result reference, and the state transition it was intended to cause. After a process restart, reconstruct pending operations and reconcile uncertain effects. This turns recovery from vague conversational memory into a controlled continuation. For long tasks, checkpoint the task state and artifacts separately from the model transcript.

A useful success report cites evidence of completion: the updated record identifier, test result, saved file, or fresh application state. It should distinguish completed work from intended work and observed facts from model inference. This is not merely a presentation convention. It closes the feedback loop and makes hidden failures discoverable by the user or evaluator.

13. Comparative evidence: read the experimental contract

Method / experimentReported comparisonWhat it supportsWhat prevents a universal ranking
ToT, GPT-4 Game of 2474% strongest ToT setting versus 4% reported CoTIntermediate search can help a structured combinatorial taskMore calls, task-specific thought granularity and evaluator
LATS, GPT-3.5 HotpotQA subsetReAct 0.32 EM; LATS ReAct 0.63; combined CoT+ReAct 0.71Search plus observations/reflection improves this feedback-rich setting100 questions, up to 50 trajectories, oracle answer feedback
SWE-agent, GPT-4 Turbo SWE-bench Lite18.0% versus 11.0% shell-only agentInterface design can materially improve the same model's executionHistorical model, fixed harness, finite task sample
Agentless, revised paper SWE-bench Lite32.0%, $0.70 average, GPT-4oA structured pipeline can be a strong efficient baselineOther table rows use different models/versions; not a matched universal comparison
τ-bench historical GPT-4o61.2% retail, 35.2% airline, 48.2% domain-weighted averageTool/dialogue/policy tasks expose substantial unreliabilitySimulator and task domains; scores are from the 2024 study
ToolOrchestra, text-only HLE37.1 versus 35.1 GPT-5 with basic tools; reported cost/latency lower across HLE+FRAMESA trained router can use a heterogeneous toolbox efficientlyThe 8B controller calls larger models; fixed paper-era prices and tool set

The research question should determine the comparison. If studying a new memory policy, hold the model and tool budget fixed and compare with no memory, raw-history retrieval, and a simpler summary baseline. If studying multi-agent coordination, compare with one agent given the same total model calls and with independent sampling plus selection. If studying a learned router, compare with cheapest-only, strongest-only, random, and a simple confidence-based escalation policy.

AI Agents That Matter argues for cost-aware evaluation and reproducibility because unconstrained accuracy encourages expensive systems and hides which components create value. Report the full quality-cost curve rather than one chosen operating point. Include model versions, input/output tokens, cache accounting, tool fees, latency distribution, and failures. API dollar cost is time-dependent; retain token counts so later readers can recompute it under new prices. [31]

An evaluation protocol for a new agent idea

Define task success in terms of observable state or a defensible answer checker. Partition tasks by meaningful difficulty, such as number of dependencies, required tools, ambiguity, and irreversible actions. Hold out new environments or compositions if claiming generalization. Repeatedly evaluate stochastic policies so that the result includes uncertainty and consistency rather than one favorable run.

Instrument failure stages: goal interpretation, evidence retrieval, planning, tool selection, argument grounding, execution, observation interpretation, memory update, integration, and stopping. A final failure can originate many steps earlier. Keep the trace and environment snapshot needed to reproduce it. Then ablate the proposed component and inspect whether it fixes the intended stage or merely shifts work elsewhere.

Track resource allocation over time. A search method may waste most calls after the first correct candidate because its selector cannot recognize success. A memory method may reduce generation tokens while increasing retrieval and context tokens. A multi-agent method may accelerate independent work but create a long integration tail. These measurements turn an appealing architecture diagram into an explanation of real performance.

14. A design synthesis: improve the weakest link in the loop

Observed failureLikely bottleneckTargeted research direction
Confident answer without required evidenceInformation acquisition and groundingRetrieval policy, source verification, explicit uncertainty
Correct plan, wrong click or file editPerception/action interfaceACI design, visual grounding, fresh state observations
Repeatedly explores the same dead endSearch diversity and state trackingAlternative proposals, visited-state memory, better terminal feedback
Reflection grows but performance does notUninformative or incorrect lessonsMatched retry ablation, evidence-backed memory, pruning
Long tasks fail despite good short tasksCompounding errors and missing recoveryCheckpoints, subgoal verification, durable state, reusable skills
Team agrees on a wrong resultCorrelated errors and weak evaluationIndependent evidence, executable checks, measured diversity
RL reward rises but real tasks worsenReward misspecification or environment overfittingIndependent evaluation, hidden tests, broader task distribution
Router always chooses one expensive modelPoor competence/cost signal or routing collapseSkill-conditioned estimates, calibrated escalation, varied costs
High pass@k but low repeat reliabilitySelection assumptions hide stochastic failurepass^k, false-success rate, consistent recovery measurement
Correct isolated steps, wrong final stateDependency/consistency failureTransactional execution, explicit contracts, end-state checks

The enduring insight is that the agent is the model plus its information, interfaces, control logic, memory, and feedback. Progress occurs when a method removes a specific bottleneck in that coupled system. ReAct makes observations affect reasoning; Toolformer learns useful triggers; ToT and LATS allocate search; memory methods preserve experience; ACI work makes actions legible; learned policies and routers optimize behavior under feedback. The next question is always which assumption allows the improvement, how the original experiment tested it, and whether that assumption holds in the task you actually need to solve.

Primary papers and official technical documents. Dates identify first reports or publication, not a claim of independent reproduction. Numerical results retain their original conditions.
